guard_patterns.handling: Require directly accessible official public source.
Keep territorial, residence and consumption accounting bases distinct.
Keep energy use, traffic, fuel supply and infrastructure distinct from emissions.
Retain reference year, publication date and lag.
Retain sample, threshold and coverage limits.
Keep certificates/obligations distinct from physical fuel or emissions.
No parcel value without verified geometry, identity, activity and method binding.
Every generated control must pass deterministic scope review.

packages.title: ONS residence-basis 2024 emissions QA
facts: ONS Environmental Accounts report 478 MtCO2e on a residence basis in 2024.
Residence basis includes UK residents and UK-registered businesses wherever activity occurs.
Foreign visitors and foreign businesses in the UK are excluded from residence basis.
Residence basis aligns with GDP and GVA concepts.
Households were the largest single contributor in 2024 at 25.9%.
Industries together made up 74.1% of residence-based emissions.
Residence-based emissions are not territorial emissions.
Residence-based emissions are not consumption-footprint emissions.
Residence-based industry values are not parcel totals.
Parcel attribution requires a separate local binding method.

packages.title: ONS transport-industry and air-transport share QA
facts: Transport was the highest-emitting industry in the 2024 residence-based accounts.
Transport industry emissions were about 78 MtCO2e in 2024.
That represented 16.3% of the total residence-based emissions.
The transport industry includes multiple transport modes.
Air transport accounted for 51.6% of transport-industry emissions in 2024.
Air transport emissions were about 40 MtCO2e in 2024.
Residence-based air transport includes UK-based airlines operating around the world.
This basis is not equivalent to UK territorial aviation emissions.
Industry transport values do not identify road links or parcels.
Mode and accounting basis must remain explicit.

packages.title: ONS direct Scope-1 boundary QA
facts: ONS Air Emission Accounts include direct residence-based emissions.
ONS describes these direct emissions as Scope 1 under GHG Protocol terminology.
Indirect electricity-chain emissions are not added to an industry's direct residence-based figure.
Household direct emissions include travel and non-travel fuel use.
Direct and supply-chain emissions must not be silently merged.
Residence Scope 1 is different from a consumption footprint.
Residence Scope 1 is different from territorial inventory geography.
A direct industry value does not establish a site-level measurement.
A site-level value does not establish a parcel-level allocation.
Accounting boundary must travel with every candidate row.

packages.title: ONS greenhouse-gas intensity trend QA
facts: ONS reports UK GHG intensity fell between 1990 and 2024.
The reported fall is 72% over that period.
The intensity metric fell from about 500 to 140 tonnes CO2e per £1 million GVA.
The metric relates emissions to economic output.
Intensity is not the same as absolute emissions.
Intensity can fall while activity composition changes.
The metric is national/economy-wide rather than parcel-specific.
GVA denominators must remain explicit.
Intensity must not be substituted for physical emissions at a site.
Parcel use requires direct local evidence rather than national intensity.

packages.title: ONS direct-energy mix 2024 QA
facts: ONS reports fossil fuels remained the largest source of direct energy consumption.
Fossil fuels accounted for 77.7% of direct energy consumption in the cited 2024 accounts.
Renewable energy accounted for 15.3%.
Direct energy consumption is an activity measure.
Energy-source shares are not themselves CO2e values.
Energy-source shares are not supplier-specific fuel-mix disclosure.
Energy-source shares are not parcel-specific consumption.
Conversion to emissions needs compatible factors and boundaries.
Reference year must remain 2024 for these shares.
Parcel emissions remain unbound without local energy and method evidence.

packages.title: ONS household travel/heating emissions QA
facts: ONS reports households were the largest single source in the residence accounts from 2015 onward.
Households accounted for 25.9% in 2024.
Main household contributors include domestic travel, particularly driving.
Home heating is another main household contributor.
Travel and non-travel household emissions were similar in scale in 2024.
Travel-related household emissions are almost entirely road transport in this account.
Household account values are residence-based.
Household account values do not identify individual homes.
Heating contribution does not imply a building-specific emission value.
Building or parcel assignment needs matched property and activity evidence.

packages.title: NEED linked meter-property method QA
facts: Domestic NEED links meter-level electricity and gas consumption to domestic properties.
NEED also links property characteristics.
NEED also links household characteristics.
The framework supports analysis of energy use and energy efficiency.
The 2026 report uses consumption data through 2024.
The publication covers domestic properties for the cited analysis.
Linked records are evidence of household energy consumption, not GHG measurements.
Energy consumption can support emissions calculation only with compatible factors.
A domestic property record is not automatically a cadastral parcel record.
Parcel binding needs an independent geometry and identity match.

packages.title: NEED on-site generation exclusion QA
facts: Domestic NEED consumption estimates represent gross household gas and grid-electricity consumption.
The cited estimates do not account for electricity generated on-site.
Solar generation at the property can therefore be outside the gross grid-consumption measure.
Electricity exported to the grid is also not incorporated in the cited gross-consumption estimate.
Grid consumption and total household energy balance are different concepts.
A solar-equipped home's NEED grid value is not its net electricity demand.
A grid-consumption value is not a GHG value by itself.
On-site generation must not be inferred from low grid consumption.
Technology presence needs separate evidence.
Parcel emissions require a complete and explicit energy boundary.

packages.title: NEED consumption-threshold coverage QA
facts: Domestic NEED applies recorded-consumption inclusion ranges.
Matched gas households are included when annual gas use is between 100 and 50,000 kWh in the cited methodology.
Matched electricity households are included when annual electricity use is between 100 and 25,000 kWh.
Only matched meter/property records enter these consumption estimates.
Houses and flats are included in the cited domestic analysis.
Other domestic property types such as caravans and house boats are excluded.
Thresholded statistics do not describe every domestic property.
Coverage constraints must be preserved in downstream use.
Out-of-range households must not be imputed from the published summary without a method.
Parcel values cannot be fabricated for excluded or unmatched properties.

packages.title: NEED mean-versus-median interpretation QA
facts: The NEED report uses median consumption in its summary analysis.
DESNZ states median is generally a better indicator of typical consumption than the mean.
The mean can be influenced by a small number of high-consuming households.
Mean and median therefore serve different interpretation purposes.
A local-authority mean must not be labelled a typical property without qualification.
A median is still a group statistic, not a specific property's reading.
Summary statistics cannot identify a parcel's actual use.
Property characteristics can correlate with consumption without uniquely determining it.
Consumption summary values need explicit aggregation labels.
Parcel emissions require actual matched activity or a declared estimation method.

packages.title: NEED local-authority table reference-year guard QA
facts: NEED 2026 consumption tables include headline England and Wales 2024 consumption tables.
The same publication also exposes local-authority tables with an older reference year for some detailed outputs.
The local-authority table listed on the 2026 page is England and Wales 2020.
Publication year and data reference year therefore differ for some tables.
A 2026 page date must not be used as the data year.
Local-authority means and medians are aggregated statistics.
Local-authority tables include property and household characteristics.
Local-authority aggregates are not parcel measurements.
Reference-year lag must be retained in the web row.
Parcel use requires a more specific source and matching step.

packages.title: NEED impact-of-measures estimated-savings QA
facts: NEED 2026 impact tables assess home energy-efficiency measures.
The tables report estimated consumption savings associated with installed measures.
Measures include loft insulation.
Published tables also cover cavity-wall insulation.
Published tables also cover solid-wall insulation.
Published tables also cover solar PV.
The impact analysis uses matched/analytical methods rather than direct parcel GHG sensing.
Estimated consumption savings are not measured CO2e savings by themselves.
Conversion to emissions requires an explicit factor and energy boundary.
A measure's average estimated impact must not be assigned to an arbitrary parcel.

packages.title: NEED anonymised sample-scope QA
facts: DESNZ publishes anonymised NEED record-level data for 2026.
A 50,000-row sample is available.
A larger 4-million-row sample is also available.
The two files are samples of the NEED dataset rather than a cadastral inventory.
Metadata describes included fields.
The records include gas and electricity consumption information.
They include property characteristics and efficiency-measure information.
Anonymisation means records must not be treated as public exact-address parcel records.
Sample membership must not be extrapolated as direct evidence for a named parcel.
Parcel binding remains a separate restricted identity/geometry problem.

packages.title: NEED property-versus-cadastral-parcel guard QA
facts: NEED is organised around domestic property and household-linked energy data.
Its purpose is energy-use and efficiency analysis.
A domestic property may not map one-to-one to a land parcel.
Flats can share a cadastral parcel or building footprint.
A parcel can contain multiple properties or meters.
Meter identity and parcel identity are different keys.
Household attributes are not land-boundary attributes.
Property-level consumption therefore cannot be assigned to a parcel without a verified crosswalk.
Aggregation must not hide one-to-many relationships.
Parcel GHG remains null until identity and geometry are explicitly verified.

packages.title: DfT road-link counted-versus-estimated QA
facts: DfT road traffic downloads expose estimation_method fields.
Road-link figures marked Counted are likely to be more accurate than those marked Estimated.
Estimated link values should be used with caution.
The website also exposes a more detailed estimation-method field.
Quality status therefore travels with each road-link estimate.
A traffic estimate is activity data, not CO2e by itself.
A counted road-link flow is still not a parcel emission measurement.
Link traffic can cross many parcels without belonging to them.
Emissions conversion requires vehicle and factor methods.
Parcel allocation requires a declared spatial allocation rule.

packages.title: DfT small-area road-quality guard QA
facts: DfT states national and regional traffic estimates are robust accredited official statistics.
Individual road-link and small-area estimates are less robust.
Individual links are not always based on up-to-date counts at those exact locations.
Local highway data can sometimes be more accurate for a specific location.
Published use should note road-link limitations.
Road-link precision must not be inflated from national quality status.
Traffic activity does not directly quantify greenhouse-gas emissions.
Small-area uncertainty should be retained in candidate confidence.
Link estimates should not be treated as measured parcel activity.
Parcel emissions require additional local evidence and allocation methodology.

packages.title: DfT road-traffic count methodology QA
facts: Annual road traffic statistics use around 7,000 roadside 12-hour manual counts.
Continuous automatic traffic counters also contribute.
Road-length data also contribute to the estimates.
The current roadtraffic site states its data were published on 20 May 2026.
The next site-data update is planned for summer 2027.
Manual and automatic observations are combined in an estimation system.
Not every road link is directly counted every year.
Method fields must be retained for link-level use.
Traffic volume must not be labelled emissions without conversion.
Parcel allocation remains a separate spatial modelling step.

packages.title: DfT SAF fifth-provisional status QA
facts: DfT published the fifth provisional SAF Mandate release on 23 July 2026.
It covers the 2025 obligation period.
The release is based on data available as of 8 July 2026.
DfT states the dataset is incomplete.
The complete finalised 2025 dataset is expected in November 2026.
The tables include low-carbon and fossil aviation fuel quantities.
The tables include SAF certificates.
They include carbon and sustainability characteristics for qualifying SAF.
Provisional fuel-supply statistics are not final aviation-emissions inventory values.
SAF supply must not be assigned to a parcel or flight without allocation evidence.

packages.title: SAF certificate-versus-physical-fuel guard QA
facts: SAF Mandate tables include SAFC certificates.
They also include physical fuel-supply quantities.
Certificate balance and fuel volume are different measures.
Certificates can be traded between suppliers and traders.
Certificate trades are not physical fuel movements.
Sustainability characteristics attach to qualifying SAF evidence.
A certificate count is not a CO2e emission quantity.
A fuel quantity still requires an emissions method to calculate GHG.
Aviation fuel supply is not a land-parcel emission record.
Downstream use must keep instrument, fuel and emissions quantities separate.

packages.title: RTFO provisional/HMRC cross-check QA
facts: DfT published the fifth provisional 2025 RTFO release on 23 July 2026.
RTFO measures renewable road and non-road mobile machinery fuel supply.
Provisional reports are revised before the final publication.
DfT states provisional fuel volumes are cross-verified with HMRC data.
Suppliers can provide data after the obligation period ends.
The collection warns provisional figures can differ from final figures.
Provisional reports should be treated as indicative rather than definitive.
The final 2025 dataset is expected in November 2026.
Fuel-supply volume is activity evidence, not a parcel CO2e measurement.
Parcel or road-link assignment requires additional activity and spatial evidence.

packages.title: RTFO versus SAF 2025 scope-separation QA
facts: The SAF Mandate came into effect for the 2025 obligation year.
SAF is excluded from the 2025 RTFO statistics series under the cited reporting change.
SAF supply is reported through the separate SAF Mandate statistics.
RTFO continues to cover renewable road and non-road mobile machinery fuels.
The two statistical series therefore have different fuel scopes.
Aviation renewable fuel must not be double-counted in 2025 RTFO totals.
Scope boundaries must be preserved when combining transport evidence.
Mandate compliance data are not territorial emissions inventories.
Fuel supply still requires lifecycle/direct-emissions interpretation.
Parcel attribution is outside both mandate statistics.

packages.title: RTFO certificate/fuel/emissions guard QA
facts: RTFO statistics report renewable fuel supply.
RTFO data also include certificate-related information.
Carbon and sustainability characteristics are reported for renewable fuel evidence.
A Renewable Transport Fuel Certificate is a compliance instrument.
Certificate quantity is distinct from physical fuel volume.
Physical fuel volume is distinct from tailpipe or lifecycle CO2e.
Provisional supplier data can be revised.
Fuel type and sustainability route must remain explicit.
National fuel supply does not identify parcel use.
Parcel emissions need separately verified local activity and conversion methods.

packages.title: Defra consumption-footprint basis QA
facts: Defra's carbon footprint measures emissions associated with UK and England consumption spending.
The footprint includes emissions wherever in the world they occur along supply chains.
It includes direct household fossil-fuel emissions from private motoring.
It includes direct household fossil-fuel emissions from heating homes.
Consumption emissions are distinct from territorial emissions.
Consumption emissions are also distinct from residence-production accounts.
The latest published series on the cited page runs to 2023.
Supply-chain emissions cannot be interpreted as local physical releases.
Consumption-footprint values are unsuitable as direct parcel measurements.
Accounting basis must be explicit before any cross-source comparison.

packages.title: Defra carbon-footprint revision-history QA
facts: Defra states historic carbon-footprint releases are superseded by each annual update.
Previous-year estimates are subject to revisions.
The current page was annually updated on 30 June 2026.
A correction was posted on 7 July 2026 to explanatory text about imports from the EU.
Historic release values should not be mixed silently with the current edition.
Revision provenance must be retained.
Consumption multipliers and source tables can change across editions.
A revision does not imply a local parcel value changed physically.
Supply-chain footprint data remain an accounting construct rather than a parcel sensor.
Only the latest verified edition should anchor current consumption-footprint QA.
